name: Minimal Traditional

geography.hearth: No design hearth. The style was standardized in Washington by the Federal Housing Administration's underwriting manuals and built simultaneously in every American metropolitan area.

lineage.note: The silhouette, the double-hung sash, the shutter, and the centred or near-centred entry survive; the proportional system, the trim profiles, and the applied orders do not. This is the most consequential partial inheritance in the American branch.

The quoted silhouette. The compact one-and-a-half storey box with a steep side gable was the FHA's most-published small house image, and the Levittown house of 1947 is a Cape reduced to its outline. It is a reference rather than a descent because the two styles are contemporaries converging in the same market rather than one transmitting practice to the other; the actual transmission of building practice runs through colonial-revival, and the reciprocal convergence is recorded on the cape-cod-revival node as a hybridization.

The vestigial front-facing entry gable with a prominent chimney beside it is a Tudor Revival move that outlived its own style, surviving as the single compositional event on thousands of otherwise plain elevations.

Not an aesthetic reaction but a cost reaction, and the more instructive for it. Every expensive element of the bungalow — the 30-inch overhang, the deep porch, the masonry piers, the built-in cabinetry, the 5-inch casing — is deleted in turn between 1930 and 1940, while the plan efficiency the bungalow pioneered is kept.

description.short: The smallest complete house the American mortgage system could underwrite: traditional in silhouette, symmetrical enough to be legible, and stripped of overhang, porch, profile depth, and every other element that cost money — the direct ancestor of the ranch and the moment the traditional kit of parts was cost-engineered out of the American house.
description.long:
Minimal Traditional is the most consequential and least discussed style in American housing. Between the middle of the 1930s and about 1950 it was built in the millions; it set the physical template for the postwar suburb; it established the dimensional habits — the shallow eave, the thin trim, the small opening, the eight-foot plate — that still govern American production housing ninety years later. It has no theorists, no manifesto, no monograph, and no architect's name attached to it. It has a federal agency instead. The house is a compact rectangle or shallow L of 750 to 1,300 square feet, one storey or one and a half, under a gable or hip of four to six in twelve. The eave and rake overhang is six to twelve inches and sometimes zero. There is no porch, only a stoop, occasionally under a small hood. The trim is a two-and-a-quarter-inch clamshell casing and a flat frieze board. The ornament consists of a chimney, a pair of shutters, and, if the budget allowed, a simple door surround. Everything else that a traditional house had was removed, deliberately, one line item at a time.

The machinery that produced it is documentable to an unusual degree, which is why this node earns a long entry. The National Housing Act of 1934 created the Federal Housing Administration to insure mortgages, and in doing so replaced the five-year balloon loan requiring fifty percent down with the amortized twenty- and later thirty-year loan requiring ten. That single change moved the binding constraint on a house from total price to monthly payment, and it moved design authority from the builder and the plan book to the underwriter. The FHA then wrote down what it would insure: Minimum Property Requirements, the underwriting manual, and a series of technical bulletins of which No. 4, Principles of Planning Small Houses (1936), is the crucial document — a national specification for the American house, complete with minimum room dimensions, circulation diagrams, and approved elevations. Because the appraisal determined the loan, and the appraisal rewarded conventional appearance and marketability, style became a risk category. Traditional silhouette was the safe collateral. This is the precise mechanism by which the traditional look survived the disappearance of traditional substance: the underwriter would insure a house that looked like a Colonial and would not insure one that looked experimental, but nothing in the underwriting manual required an eave, a porch, or a moulding with depth. The same apparatus, it must be said plainly, wrote redlining into the national housing map, and the Minimal Traditional landscape is inseparable from that fact.

The cost engineering itself follows a legible sequence, and any design system for production housing should study it, because the same sequence runs today. Overhang goes first: it consumes rafter length, sheathing, soffit material, fascia, flashing, gutter, and labour at height, and its benefit — shadow, weather protection of the wall, and a visible termination for the roof — is invisible on a spec sheet. The porch goes second, because it is conditioned-area-equivalent cost with no conditioned area. Trim profile depth goes third: a two-and-a-quarter-inch clamshell costs a third of a four-and-a-half-inch moulded casing and, unlike the casing, casts no shadow. Wall thickness, window size, and ceiling height follow. Wartime accelerated all of it: the Linda Vista defense project in San Diego put up three thousand houses in two hundred and fifty-nine days in 1941-43, and by 1947 Levitt was building a 750-square-foot Cape on a 60-by-100-foot lot in twenty-six sequenced operations, thirty a day. The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944 supplied the demand. What survived the process is exactly what cost nothing: proportion of the overall mass, placement of the openings, and the outline against the sky.

And here is the part that resists the lament. These are, at their best, decent little houses, and a street of them reads better than most of what has been built since. The plans are tight and workable, the rooms are small but correctly related, the massing is compact, and — critically — the kit was so short that consistency was almost unavoidable, so the street has a coherence that no amount of variety-seeking has since reproduced. Minimal Traditional is the proof that a coherent public realm can be made from an impoverished kit of parts provided the rules are few, consistent, and universally followed. Standing in front of one you feel the absence physically: the wall meets the sky at a knife edge with no shadow at all, the door sits in the plane of the wall with no reveal, the shutters are half the width of the window and could never have closed, and there is nowhere to stand out of the rain. But you also feel that nothing is pretending. The house is exactly as big as it is, and it does not have a two-storey entry, and the roof is one simple shape. Between this house and the neo-eclectic house of 1985 the money spent per square foot went up substantially and the quality of the street went down, which is the single most useful fact in this entire branch of the graph.

defining_characteristics: Compact rectangular or shallow-L massing of 750 to 1,300 sq ft, one storey or one and a half, with the long axis often perpendicular to the street
Moderate roof pitch of 4:12 to 6:12, gabled or hipped, with eave and rake overhang not exceeding 12 in and frequently under 6 in
Complete absence of a habitable porch; entry is a stoop, at most under a small hood or shallow entry gable
Ornament reduced to three items at most: a chimney, a pair of decorative shutters, and a simple door surround
Trim of minimal profile depth — flat frieze, narrow clamshell or ranch casing, no cornice return of any consequence
Small double-hung openings, six-over-six or two-over-two, sized and placed by interior requirement rather than by facade composition
Traditional silhouette retained as the only surviving carrier of style: the outline is Colonial or Cape, and nothing below the outline is
diagnostic_tells: A recognizably traditional shape with essentially no eave — the roof surface stops at the wall surface and the two meet without a shadow line
Shutters roughly half the width of the sash they flank, fixed flat to the wall
The front door lies in the plane of the wall with a reveal of an inch or less and no projecting surround
A single small gabled or hipped entry projection or bay as the only three-dimensional event on the whole elevation
One-and-a-half storey examples carrying an added shed dormer at the rear, from a later expansion of the attic

distinguished_from.difference: Cape Cod Revival keeps the full symmetrical five-bay facade, the heavier trim, the correct cornice with returns, and a genuine central chimney. Minimal Traditional keeps the box and deletes all four. The tell is the rake: a Cape Cod Revival has a moulded rake with a return at the eave; Minimal Traditional has a 1x6 board.

The ranch is longer than it is deep, sits lower, has a wider eave, opens its plan, and attaches its garage. Minimal Traditional is an upright compact block with a cellular plan and a detached garage at the rear of the lot, reached by a driveway beside the house.

The same size and often the same footprint, thirty years apart. The bungalow has a 30-inch eave, a full-width porch, exposed rafters, and built-in cabinetry; Minimal Traditional has none of them. If it is small and has a deep porch it is a bungalow; if it is small and has a stoop it is Minimal Traditional.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Economic, not proportional, and it is important to say so without apology because it is the true answer. The governing modules are the FHA minimum room dimension, the 16-inch stud bay, the 8-foot precut stud and the 8-foot ceiling that follows from it, the 4-by-8 sheet, and the maximum insurable loan amount. The facade is a residual: openings are located by the rooms behind them and then nudged toward apparent balance. Nothing is derived from a module of order, and the style's visual coherence comes not from any internal system but from the smallness and uniformity of its vocabulary.
typical_ratios: Overall footprint 24 x 32 ft to 26 x 40 ft
Roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12; eave and rake overhang 0 to 12 in
Wall plate 8 ft 0 in; window and door head 6 ft 8 in
Window openings 2 ft 8 in to 3 ft 0 in wide by 4 ft 2 in to 4 ft 10 in tall, roughly 1:1.6
Casing 2 1/4 in wide with a projection under 3/4 in
FHA minimum principal bedroom approximately 9 ft 6 in by 11 ft 0 in
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and plan-driven. Openings occur in ones and twos with no governing interval; the appearance of rhythm on the best examples is the result of a two-room-deep plan happening to produce even spacing.

massing_affinities.note: The one-and-a-half storey side-gabled box; the FHA's most-published and Levitt's chosen form.
The single-storey version with a projecting entry or living-room gable — the one compositional move the style allows itself.
The transitional form of 1948-1953: the same detailing stretched along the lot. Watching this massing displace cape-cod-massing in a subdivision's build-out sequence dates it to within two years.
The two-room single-storey core of the smallest wartime examples is literally this ancient skeleton, arrived at again by cost rather than by tradition.

constraints.statement: Eave and rake overhang shall not exceed 12 in. Where overhang exceeds 12 in the node is misassigned; classify as cape-cod-revival, colonial-revival, or ranch-style.

test.note: The statement gives one shared 12in ceiling for both eave and rake overhang; eave_projection_in stands in for the general overhang measurement since no separate rake-overhang variable exists in the vocabulary.

constraints.statement: Conditioned floor area 750 to 1,400 sq ft; roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12; one or one and a half storeys only.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch clause. Conditioned floor area (750-1,400 sq ft) has no vocabulary variable (missing: floor_area_sqft) and stays prose; storey count ('one or one and a half storeys only') is separately expressible via the existing storey_count variable as one-of ["1","1.5"] but only one test object is permitted per constraint, so it also stays prose here.

constraints.statement: Decorative shutters, where used, must each be not less than 45 percent of the width of the window opening they flank, hinged at the jamb, and must be omitted entirely from ganged, bay, and non-rectangular windows. Half-width shutters are the single most common failure of this style's descendants and are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the minimum leaf-width ratio. Hinge position and the omission-from-ganged/bay/non-rectangular-window rule are categorical and stay prose.

constraints.statement: No full- or partial-width habitable porch. Entry cover projection not more than 3 ft; where a deeper covered space is wanted the node is not minimal-traditional.

test.note: Tests the entry-cover projection ceiling. 'No full- or partial-width habitable porch' is a qualitative prohibition and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Room dimensions follow FHA Minimum Property Requirements as a historical floor: principal bedroom not less than 9 ft 6 in by 11 ft 0 in, secondary bedroom not less than 8 ft 0 in by 10 ft 0 in, minimum one full bath.

exemplars.name: Linda Vista Defense Housing Project
exemplars.note: 3,000 houses and 750 dormitory units built in 259 days, 1941-43, at up to 40 completions a day, under a garden-city neighbourhood plan. The style's wartime proving ground.
exemplars.why: The style's largest single wartime population, and the only one whose houses a contemporary source dimensioned -- 25 by 30 feet, 750 square feet, in The San Diego Union of 23 March 1941 -- which is a reporter's figure rather than a surveyor's, and is why it stands here as documentary.

exemplars.name: Levittown
exemplars.note: The 1947 Levitt Cape: roughly 750 sq ft on a 60 x 100 ft lot, built in 26 sequenced operations. Over 17,000 houses by 1951, sold to veterans under the GI Bill at about $8,000 with almost nothing down.
exemplars.why: The development every account of American postwar housing reaches for first, and the one this node's own cited sources -- Jackson, Wright, Lane -- all treat as the type case.

exemplars.name: Westlake, Daly City
exemplars.note: Henry Doelger's tract, begun in the late 1940s and built out through the 1950s. The West Coast counterpart, and the place where the style visibly shades into the ranch mid-subdivision. Construction begins 1949; the tract was annexed to Daly City in 1948.
exemplars.why: The West Coast counterpart, and the tract that the statewide context statement Tract Housing in California, 1945-1973 uses to illustrate BOTH the Postwar Minimal house and the tract Ranch, which is the shading into ranch-style this exemplar's note describes.

exemplars.name: East Alvarado Historic District
exemplars.note: Thirty houses on a quarter mile of one street between Third and Seventh, listed on the National Register expressly as a representation of Federal Housing Administration policy on subdivision development in the late 1930s. Its nomination describes the eave and the shutter in the terms this node's kit uses -- 'little, if any, overhang', 'false shutters, usually louvered' -- and calls the same houses 'Early Ranch' or Minimal Traditional interchangeably, which is a boundary this corpus draws and Phoenix does not.
exemplars.why: A documented type specimen at the scale of a street: a National Register nomination that names the style, states the FHA mechanism this node's description rests on, and describes thirty examples of it, on the judgment of the City of Phoenix's own multiple-property documentation of 1994.

exemplars.name: Richmond Heights Pioneer Historic District
exemplars.note: The first twenty-six houses of a development built for African American veterans of the Second World War under segregation, all sold in December 1949 and grown to 457 houses by 1951. Concrete block with plain stucco, mostly three bedrooms, on lots measuring 75 by 100 feet -- the minimal-traditional house built as masonry in a hot-humid climate, which the node's frame-wall description does not cover.
exemplars.why: The Gulf and South Atlantic expression of the type, in the one construction the node's own description never contemplates, and the listing is the National Park Service's, announced by the Florida Department of State, whose press release is the page this record carries.

exemplars.name: Ervin and Ethel Jesse House
exemplars.note: 7402 Eads Avenue: one ordinary Minimal Traditional house read feature by feature against the FHA's own Principles of Planning Small Houses in a City of San Diego historic resource report. A gable-and-wing sub-type -- a low-pitched front gable added to one side of a side-gabled roof, projecting barely at all in front of it.
exemplars.why: The only single house among these exemplars, and the only document that holds the FHA pamphlet this node argues from against a real building; the judgment is the report's author's, and the record states that the Historical Resources Board's decision on it was not read, so no City of San Diego designation is claimed.

sources: Federal Housing Administration, Principles of Planning Small Houses, Technical Bulletin No. 4 (1936)
Kenneth T. Jackson, Crabgrass Frontier: The Suburbanization of the United States (1985)
Gwendolyn Wright, Building the Dream: A Social History of Housing in America (1981)
Barbara Miller Lane, Houses for a New World: Builders and Buyers in American Suburbs, 1945-1965 (2015)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)

proportion_packs.note: The FHA minimum room dimensions this node's own constraint c05 states as a historical floor (principal bedroom not less than 9 ft 6 in x 11 ft 0 in, secondary not less than 8 ft 0 in x 10 ft 0 in) and its governing_logic's own claim ('nothing is derived from a module of order') land inside this pack's reconstructed vernacular band -- span-, hearth- (obsolete by this date, replaced by forced air) and daylight-limited rooms clustering at a 1.0-1.5 ratio -- rather than anywhere in the treatise literature this pack is deliberately the counterweight to. The FHA principal bedroom's 9 ft 6 in breadth sits below even this pack's own 11 ft floor for a principal room, which is itself the diagnostic: this is the vernacular room logic pushed one further notch toward the economic minimum, continuing exactly the deletion sequence the node's own lineage entry against craftsman describes.

The style's own defining_characteristics name '6/6 or 2/2' sash directly, which is precisely the light pattern this pack's derived rules emit for cheap, large, early-to-mid-20th-century glass, and the node's constraint c03 (shutter leaf not less than 45 percent of sash width, hinged at the jamb, forbidden on ganged/bay/non-rectangular windows) quotes this pack's own shutter rule almost verbatim. Bound ahead of opening-proportion per this pack's own stated precedence over that one where the two disagree.

Retained for the single-head-datum rule, which still organizes what compositional discipline the elevation has ('the appearance of rhythm on the best examples is the result of a two-room-deep plan happening to produce even spacing'). FLAGGED DEVIATION: the node's own typical_ratios give openings 2 ft 8 in-3 ft 0 in wide by 4 ft 2 in-4 ft 10 in tall -- roughly 1.5:1 to 1.8:1 -- markedly squarer than this pack's canonical 13:6 (2.167:1) and below its documented range floor of 1.75:1, a real measured consequence of the 6 ft 8 in head and 8 ft 0 in plate the governing_logic names. No pack in the library currently states this compressed ratio as its own default; worth flagging for WP-4.6.

Bound as the closest available system, not a close fit. The node's own casing -- 2 1/4 in wide, under 3/4 in projection -- is thinner than even this pack's stated economy floor ('below 3 1/2 in the family stops working, because the head casing has nowhere to overhang to'), so what Minimal Traditional actually built is a further reduction beyond what any pack in this library describes as the cheapest classical-adjacent system. Bound optional and low: the flat-stock, order-indifferent logic is directionally correct, but no pack currently states a system thin enough to describe a 2 1/4 in clamshell casing without extrapolating past its own documented range. Worth flagging for WP-4.6.

declined_packs.reason: A rule for graduating a stack of storeys has no stack to graduate. This node's own record makes a single storey (or one and a half) definitional, so `height_proportion` arriving as a second-to-first-storey ratio dimensions a floor the house does not have.
declined_packs.quote: one storey or one and a half
declined_packs.note: Declined, not merely unendorsed: the pack reached this node through the cascade and nobody had ever judged it. `--impact` first — on ranch-style the pack governs one interior slot and nothing is left undimensioned; on craftsman-bungalow it governs none.

declined_packs.reason: gibbs-ionic's own notes call it a delta on Vignola whose every figure is stated in parts of "the semidiameter of the column at its base" - the module of the order is the pack's whole subject, not an incidental of it. The node's governing_logic denies that module by name and puts the FHA room minimum, the 16-inch stud bay and the 8-foot precut stud in its place, and the three slots the pack governs here are order members: it delivers a six-inch Georgian Ionic architrave to a house whose own typical_ratios state a 2 1/4 in casing, and a pilaster projection to a front whose tells say the door "lies in the plane of the wall ... with no projecting surround". The lineage entry to colonial-revival says the same thing from the other side - silhouette, sash, shutter and entry survive, "the applied orders do not". This is not the blanket-sentence trap: the node's sentence names the pack's own stated mechanism, term for term.
declined_packs.quote: Nothing is derived from a module of order
declined_packs.note: Governs 3 slots: casing, cornice, pilaster. 0 slots lose all dimensioning. But the decline is nearly inert numerically and that is worth recording: casing passes to palladio-tuscan and cornice to chambers-ionic at BYTE-IDENTICAL expressions (`opening_width / 6` and `storey_height / 4 * (7 / 18)`), because the sixth-of-the-opening architrave rule is common to the treatises. Only pilaster's figure actually moves, `column_height / 18` -> `5 / 6` (chambers-ionic). A decline stops this pack; it does not stop the order. It also keeps `gibbs_order_applies_to_style` false on this node, which given OQ 84's discriminator trap is the honest state.

declined_packs.reason: trim-classical's derivation paragraph is its subject in one line - "A room is an order at reduced scale" - with base, dado, chair rail, wall and cornice read as plinth, die, pedestal cap, column and entablature, dividing 4 : 12 : 3 in nineteenths off Vignola. The node's own record refuses both halves of that: it says in its lineage entry that the trim profiles and the proportional system do not come down from colonial-revival while the silhouette and sash do, and its governing_logic says nothing is derived from a module of order. The pack's own honest qualification points the same way and independently - it marks the eight-foot ceiling a BLOCKING conflict ("at eight feet it puts it at 20 in, which is nonsense"), and eight feet is precisely the plate this node states.
declined_packs.quote: the proportional system, the trim profiles, and the applied orders do not
declined_packs.note: Governs 4 slots: baseboard, crown, interior_door, wainscot. 0 slots lose all dimensioning - and, measured, the decline changes NO figure at all. All four slots carry an inherited slot-level `packs` ruling naming trim-classical at precedence 1 with its own expression, so `choose_pack` takes the `slot.packs` branch and returns the identical number with the pack undelivered (`ceiling_height * 1.5 / 19`, `* 1.2 / 19`, `* 0.7`, `* 1.92 / 19`). The --impact line "-> trim-classical (None)" is that stale ruling surfacing, not a fallback pack - the same class already visible on ranch-style / storey-graduation, and OQ 87's shape. The decline is correct on the record but does not bite until those four inherited slot rulings are worked.

declined_packs.reason: timber-bay's module is one structural bay of a box frame - centre of one bent to the centre of the next, bounded below by the smallest habitable room and above by the span a hewn 4 x 8 joist will make, so 16 to 20 feet - and its own test is "can you draw the frame?", with the partitions and window jambs falling near the posts. The node names its governing modules outright and every one of them is light-frame: a 16-INCH stud bay, an 8-foot precut stud, a 4-by-8 sheet; bay_rhythm adds that openings occur "in ones and twos with no governing interval". The number 16 appears in both records and means inches in one and feet in the other - the second trap exactly, and here there is not even a coincidence of magnitude, only of digits. There is no bent to space.
declined_packs.quote: the 16-inch stud bay, the 8-foot precut stud and the 8-foot ceiling that follows from it, the 4-by-8 sheet
declined_packs.note: Governs 0 slots - declining changes no dimension on this node. The decline's whole value is the gate it keeps shut: endorsing would switch `span_check`'s capacity in build/structure.py from the light-frame joist table to the bay module's own, and build/geometry_cp.py reads the same list, on a house whose own record is framed in 16-inch stud bays. Given WP-7.4 left both reference plans failing their span capacity loudly, arming that swap here on an unjudged inheritance would be the wrong direction.

declined_packs.reason: facade-picturesque's own notes say what it is about in one sentence: "In a classical front the axis does the ordering ... In a picturesque front there is no axis, so the horizontals must do all of it", and its module note adds that the module is the dominant mass "because a picturesque elevation has no bay - that is the whole point of it". This node's record answers that question the other way, term for term: its symmetry field is near-symmetrical, its governing_logic says the facade's openings are "nudged toward apparent balance", and its lineage entry to colonial-revival says the centred or near-centred entry is one of the four things that survived. The pack's entry_sequence rule -- the slot that actually loses dimensioning -- is titled "DISTANCE OF THE ENTRANCE FROM THE VISUAL CENTRE" and reads "The picturesque entrance is deliberately not on the axis - there is no axis", putting the door 18 ft off centre on a house whose own typical_ratios give a 24 x 32 ft footprint. The pack's own dominance rule names this node's case as outside itself: above a ratio of 2.5 "the subordinate mass has become an appendage ... no longer picturesque composition - it is a classical block with an ell", which is exactly the tell "a single small gabled or hipped entry projection or bay as the only three-dimensional event on the whole elevation".
declined_packs.quote: the centred or near-centred entry survive
declined_packs.note: Governs 3 slots: entry_sequence, material_change_rule, roof_form. 1 slot loses all dimensioning -- entry_sequence goes to NOTHING, which is the honest state here: an 18 ft offset from the visual centre on a 24 x 32 ft near-symmetrical box is a wrong dimension, and no dimension beats it. The other two are re-supplied from elsewhere in the cascade: material_change_rule -> log-module (swiss-chalet) and roof_form -> facade-pavilion (beaux-arts-french). Neither replacement is endorsed by this node either; they are the next unjudged deliveries and stay on the OQ 51 work list. --pair reports no live gate, so this changes numbers only.

declined_packs.reason: trim-sawn's own module note states its subject as two machines rather than a period: "THE MODULE IS THE REPEAT BECAUSE THE MACHINE IS THE SUBJECT ... the scroll saw and the lathe", producing bargeboards, brackets, spindle friezes, turned posts and pierced valances, and its notes say "the pack's central rule is a COUNT of members rather than a dimension of any one of them". This node's record answers that count exhaustively and the answer excludes every member the pack names: its ornament is enumerated as three items -- a chimney, shutters and a door surround -- and the description.long says "Everything else that a traditional house had was removed, deliberately, one line item at a time." The distinguished_from entry against cape-cod-revival makes the rake explicit, which is where a bargeboard would go: "Minimal Traditional has a 1x6 board." The pack's own notes cite three records that define themselves by refusing it; this is a fourth of the same shape, and it refuses on economics rather than on taste.
declined_packs.quote: Ornament reduced to three items at most: a chimney, a pair of decorative shutters, and a simple door surround
declined_packs.note: Governs 0 slots -- declining changes no dimension on this node, and --pair reports no live gate, so nothing is armed either way. The value is that it stops a catalogue of sawn and turned members reaching a node whose own record closes its ornament list at three items, and moves the gap from unjudged to judged. Note the known consequence: a decline re-attributes the interior role to the next unjudged ancestor, so this may surface a new gap rather than close one.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own note says its proportions ARE Vignola's Ionic -- eighteen modules of column, four and a half of entablature, one of base -- and that Chambers's departures are about which form, not about how big; it dimensions balustrade, chair_rail, column, frieze, ornament_vocabulary, pilaster and porch_support off that module. The node's governing_logic answers that claim in one clause and does so deliberately, saying it is important to state the economic answer without apology: nothing here is derived from a module of order, and the governing modules are the FHA minimum room dimension, the 16-inch stud bay, the 8-foot precut stud, the 4-by-8 sheet and the maximum insurable loan. The pack governs cornice and pilaster on this node, and the record refuses both at their addresses: c01 caps eave and rake overhang at 12 in and reassigns the node if it is exceeded, its first tell is a roof surface stopping at the wall with no shadow line at all, and its only three-dimensional event on the whole elevation is a small entry projection. The node already declines gibbs-ionic on this identical sentence.
declined_packs.quote: Nothing is derived from a module of order
declined_packs.note: Delivered by english-georgian at cascade depth 10 with no direct lineage edge. Governs 2 slots: cornice, which passes to palladio-ionic (english-palladian), and pilaster, which passes to benjamin-ionic (federal-style); 0 slots lose all dimensioning. --pair reports no live gate. Stated honestly: both successors are Ionic order packs of the same family and carry the same contradiction to the same two addresses, so this decline stops one delivery and not the class. palladio-ionic and benjamin-ionic on this node are the next adjudications.
